rationale:
Every piece today is about plague, as the channel focus requires. I skipped angles we've covered in the last 30 days: the status decoder, Madagascar, lab safety, person-to-person spread, curability, US case counts, the exposure steps, CDC traveller screening, the vaccine, symptoms, the 3 forms, risk levels and the Black Death.

**Long-form (L1).** The radar's newest development is that quarantine was lifted on Oct 8 while WHO still says it lacks enough information. L1 uses that to explain the science behind standing down: incubation windows, how long contacts are watched, how plague is diagnosed, and why "nothing found in contacts tested" is not the same as "ruled out". It is new depth rather than a rerun of the 10-07 decoder, and it puts the dated status in the opening beat, as the playbook asks. S1 is a spin-off of L1.

**Mix.** Four pieces are emerging, low-competition topics, so we get there early: L1, S1, the cures myth (S2) and marmots (S3). The carousel refreshes our best format, plague plus a place plus a CDC number plus practical prevention, with a hiker and pet-owner checklist. S2 is the bold myth correction, built on AFP's Oct 9 fact check. The pieces cover different ground: lungs and timing, treatment, wildlife reservoirs, and outdoor prevention.

**Rules applied.**
- Every title starts with "Plague" or "Pneumonic plague".
- Every piece gets a dated "suspected/reported" line, credited to the body that said it.
- No self-treatment and no stockpiling.
- Every piece carries "contact a doctor or local health authority urgently" and "If you're worried, talk to a health professional."
- Re-check CDC's wording at publish time: the incubation figure (CDC is quoted as 1–4 days in one place and 1–3 in another) and the US case count (the 10-09 check read "an average of five", range 0–17).

**Not used.**
- The IHR topic carries a cover-up framing risk, so I held it.
- "Pneumonic vs bubonic" was skipped because the 3-forms carousel ran on 10-07, inside the 30-day window.

**Before publishing.**
- **Playlists:** the pillar list we received only has GLP-1 playlists. None of them fits plague, so every piece uses `general` ("Health Science Explained"). Someone should add a plague playlist before these go out.
- **Carousels still reach almost no one** (0–2 accounts on 13 posts). The C1 topic would work better as a Reel if the owner swaps the carousel slot for a Short.

pieces.topic: Why the Irkutsk quarantine ended: pneumonic plague incubation, contact monitoring windows, and how plague is diagnosed (culture, PCR, rapid tests)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Plague Case in Russia: What's Confirmed, What's Suspected and How Plague Is Diagnosed (as of Oct 10, 2026)'. Opening beat: as of Oct 8, 2026, the Irkutsk oblast governor said quarantine had been lifted, with nearly 5,000 tests finding no dangerous microorganisms and monitoring of close contacts complete (use his exact figure and wording). WHO says it has asked for more information. Russian authorities describe second-case reports as false (paraphrase, no quote marks). Plague is not confirmed and not ruled out. Then: incubation (CDC: pneumonic 'can be as short as 1 day'; WHO: 1–7 days for Y. pestis), WHO's contact monitoring and 7-day preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, lab diagnosis (culture from blood, sputum or bubo samples, PCR, the WHO-validated rapid dipstick, reference-lab confirmation), and what negative tests in contacts can and can't tell us. Close with the urgent-contact line and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Plague Quarantine Lifted in Russia: Why a Week of Watching Contacts Is Enough (as of Oct 10)
pieces.why: The quarantine lifted on Oct 8 left a gap between 'over' and 'unexplained' that people are searching to understand, with low competition. It is our first chance at a plague long-form with new depth rather than a repeat of the held decoder. | fact-check: The topic is sound and fits the pillars, but four things need fixing. (1) The title says 'Why a Week of Watching Contacts Is Enough'. That is our own judgement and no agency has said it, while WHO says it still lacks the information it needs. 'Lifted in Russia' is also too wide: the quarantine was in Irkutsk oblast. (2) CDC's signs-and-symptoms page (last reviewed May 15, 2024) says the pneumonic incubation period 'can be as short as 1 day' and gives no upper limit, so CDC can't be the source for 'about a week'. WHO's fact sheet says 'an incubation period of one to seven days' for Y. pestis in general (not specific to pneumonic). WHO also tells authorities to 'identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them a seven-day chemoprophylaxis.' Credit each fact to the body that actually says it. (3) I couldn't confirm 'over 90% of contacts' in any source. Liga, UNN and AFP report that Governor Kobzev said nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous microorganisms and that medical monitoring of all close contacts was complete. The Kyiv Independent article I found is the earlier quarantine story. Copy the governor's exact figure from a reachable source and date it to the day he said it (AFP: Thursday, Oct 8). Credit the 'community-acquired pneumonia' diagnosis to the governor, as reported. (4) Some outlets repeat a 'broken test tube' story and say she died 'from pneumonic plague' as if that were fact. Leave both out. On the 'why it ended' question, only report the reasons the governor gave. Don't invent a safety-margin rationale.

pieces.topic: Pneumonic plague incubation period: why contact observation ends after about a week
pieces.angle: Title: 'Pneumonic Plague Incubation: How Fast Symptoms Can Start (CDC and WHO) #shorts'. Answer within 10 s: CDC says pneumonic plague symptoms can start as soon as 1 day after exposure, and WHO says plague symptoms usually appear within 1 to 7 days. That's why health authorities monitor close contacts and give them a 7-day course of preventive antibiotics (WHO). Status, credited and dated: as of Oct 8, 2026, the Irkutsk oblast governor said quarantine had been lifted; WHO says it has asked for more information; plague is not confirmed and not ruled out. Close: a possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Point viewers to L1.
pieces.working_title: Pneumonic Plague Incubation: Why Contacts Are Watched for About a Week #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 that drives viewers to the long video. 'Plague incubation period' is a plain search question with low competition, timed to the quarantine news. | fact-check: The angle depends on a CDC 'window' that would justify ending observation after about a week. CDC's page doesn't give one: it only says pneumonic incubation 'can be as short as 1 day'. Neither CDC nor WHO says observation ends after about a week. WHO gives 1–7 days for Y. pestis in general and recommends 7-day chemoprophylaxis for close contacts. Don't say or imply that Irkutsk stood down because of the incubation period; that is our inference. Keep the status line dated and attributed, and list CDC's 4 pneumonic warning signs in full.

pieces.topic: Unproven plague 'cures' circulating online (AFP Fact Check, Oct 9) vs what actually treats plague
pieces.angle: Hook: 'Prepper kits and unproven pills: AFP Fact Check reports dubious plague cures spreading online (Oct 8, 2026).' Answer within 10 s: WHO says antibiotics and supportive care work against plague when it's diagnosed in time, and doctors prescribe them. Experts told AFP not to take antibiotics without a known exposure. Health authorities give preventive antibiotics to close contacts. No product names, no remedy list, no drug names or doses. Add the dated Irkutsk status hedge. Close with the urgent-contact line and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Plague Cures Online: What Actually Treats Plague, According to CDC and WHO #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Plague 'Cures' Online: What Actually Treats Plague, According to CDC and WHO #shorts
pieces.why: The bold myth-busting piece of the day. AFP published only on Oct 9, so we're early, and it builds on the 'Is plague curable?' Reel that reached 102 accounts. | fact-check: The AFP piece is real ('Unproven cures pushed online amid plague concerns', syndicated by CP24/CTV on Oct 8, 2026), but it doesn't mention garlic, herbs or home remedies. It covers influencers and preppers selling a roughly $300 kit and an X post listing supplements and drugs. Experts told AFP ivermectin would be ineffective and warned against taking antibiotics without a known exposure. The hook has to match that, and the date has to be the AFP publication date (Oct 8 per syndication, not Oct 9, unless AFP's own page says otherwise). Don't name the influencer or list the remedies. Use WHO's own wording on treatment: 'Antibiotics and supportive therapy are effective against plague if patients are diagnosed in time', and pneumonic plague 'can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours… if left untreated'. The experts' warning against taking antibiotics without exposure directly supports the no-stockpiling guardrail, so include it.

pieces.topic: Plague and marmots: why marmots, not rats, are a key plague reservoir in Siberia, Mongolia and China
pieces.angle: Title: 'Plague and Marmots: Why Marmots Matter for Plague in Mongolia and Siberia #shorts'. In natural plague foci in Mongolia and southern Siberia, marmots and their fleas, along with other wild rodents, help keep Yersinia pestis circulating. Hunting, skinning or eating infected marmots has been linked to human bubonic cases. Mongolia's NCZD reported marmot-linked cases in Aug 2026 (as reported by the Moscow Times; use their exact suspected/confirmed wording). Treat eating marmot respectfully as a cultural tradition. Prevention: don't handle sick or dead wild animals, and wear gloves if you're skinning animals (CDC). Add the dated Irkutsk status hedge with no marmot link. Close with the urgent-contact line and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Plague and Marmots: Why Marmots, Not Rats, Carry Plague in Central Asia #shorts
pieces.why: National Geographic published on this Oct 9 and nobody on YouTube links it to the news yet. It gives evergreen Plague 101 a timely hook with low competition. | fact-check: Good evergreen Plague 101 topic, but three fixes. (1) 'Marmots, not rats' overstates it. Natural plague foci in this region also involve ground squirrels, gerbils and pikas, and rats are still reservoirs elsewhere. (2) The Mongolia Aug 2026 reports aren't consistent. A Moscow Times item (themoscowtimes.com/2026/08/04) cites Mongolia's NCZD on two 'suspected' cases linked to marmot meat but also says lab tests confirmed them, and other outlets report a death in Khovd on Aug 11. Open the Moscow Times article, check its date and content, and copy its exact status wording, credited to Mongolia's NCZD as reported by the Moscow Times. (3) I couldn't verify the claim that Rospotrebnadzor has warned against marmot hunting. Source it or drop it. Keep the respectful cultural context, use no horror imagery, and make no link to Irkutsk.

pieces.topic: Plague in US national parks and the Southwest: a prevention checklist for hikers, campers and pet owners (CDC)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Plague in the US West: 5 CDC Prevention Tips for Hikers, Campers and Pet Owners'. Slide 1: 'An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the US (CDC, range 0–17; reviewed Oct 7, 2026).' Slide 2: where cases occur per CDC, plus human cases vs animal cases. Tips, each with the CDC page that says it: avoid sick or dead animals (contact your local health department about disposal); DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing; flea control for pets (add the cat-toxicity caveat only with a source); don't let free-roaming pets in endemic areas sleep on your bed; red flags after a trip, then contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention the trip. Calm fact in CDC's own wording about the 1924–25 Los Angeles epidemic. Short dated Irkutsk status line. Last slide: 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Plague in US National Parks: 6 CDC Prevention Tips for Hikers and Pet Owners
pieces.why: An evergreen topic refreshed by the Oct 7 Outside and AP coverage. It is our best-performing format (plague plus place plus CDC number plus prevention) turned into a checklist people save, with a new angle on outdoor trips rather than case counts. | fact-check: Confirmed on CDC's statistics page (reviewed Oct 7, 2026): 'An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the United States', range 0–17, with cases mainly in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada. Problems: (1) CDC doesn't mention national parks, so the title has to say 'the rural West' or 'the Southwest'. (2) CDC's pets-in-bed tip is scoped: 'Do not allow dogs or cats that roam free in endemic areas to sleep on your bed.' Keep that scope. (3) The repellent tip should match CDC: DEET on skin, permethrin on clothing, and follow the label. (4) CDC's prevention page (reviewed Mar 5, 2025) doesn't show the cat-toxicity line or the prairie-dog line in what I checked. Find a CDC page that says them, or drop them. (5) For the 1924 fact, CDC's wording is 'The last urban plague epidemic in the United States occurred in Los Angeles from 1924 through 1925.' Quote that rather than 'no person-to-person spread since 1924' unless a CDC page states the latter. (6) The title says 6 tips but the angle lists 5. (7) Carousels have reached 0–2 accounts per the playbook, so consider making this a Short.

pieces.topic: Plague vs COVID: one is a bacterium, one is a virus. How each spreads, who passes it on, how each is treated, and why public-health tools work differently against them
pieces.angle:
Keep the plan as written, with these changes.

STATUS LINE: re-check at publish time and give each line its own date and the body that said it. As of Oct 6, 2026, WHO (spokesperson Christian Lindmeier, via UN News) said authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused the death of a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died, and no official cause of death has been confirmed. Russia's Rospotrebnadzor reported 'pneumonia of unknown etiology' and said testing found no microorganisms linked to the patient's work. Use the date Rospotrebnadzor gave that statement, not the date an article was published. Russian authorities reported no dangerous pathogens among contacts, and none had symptoms. Not confirmed isn't ruled out. Put the newest development first. If you use WHO's risk assessment, quote it exactly ('moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region'), credited to WHO on Oct 6, 2026.

ROW 2: use CDC's wording, 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people', for pneumonic plague. Bubonic and septicemic plague come from flea bites or from handling an infected animal (CDC).

ROW 3: 'Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague' (CDC; mention sick cats as CDC's example). Don't claim plague is 'not airborne at all'. Just contrast it with CDC's description of COVID spreading through shared air, including from people without symptoms.

ROW 4: plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early' (CDC/WHO). No drug names or doses. Say nothing about a plague vaccine. For COVID, just say that CDC lists vaccines and antiviral treatments.

ROW 5: use CDC's exact line, 'Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.'

CLOSE: as planned, using CDC's 4 pneumonic signs: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Then 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'

Title: 'Plague vs COVID: How Each Spreads and Why They're So Different' is fine. Thumbnail: a labelled bacterium and virus, no doom words, no patient, no skulls or rats.
pieces.working_title: Plague vs COVID: How Each Spreads and Why They're So Different
pieces.why:
Replaces the dropped L1. It's a rising, evergreen comparison that names both sides, can be checked against stable CDC/WHO pages, and avoids the diagnostics wording and dated-statement problems that got L1 held. | fact-check: Good evergreen topic. It names both sides, sticks to agency sources and matches the 'Plague vs COVID: how each spreads' item on the playbook. The core facts check out against primary sources. Three things need fixing before scripting.

(1) The planned status line is out of date and too weak. Since the plan was written, Rospotrebnadzor has reported that the worker was diagnosed with 'pneumonia of unknown etiology'. It also said that 'based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample' (Snopes, Oct 5, 2026). The UN News piece of Oct 6, 2026 quotes WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier: authorities 'are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death', no official cause of death has been confirmed, all contacts were identified and monitored with none showing symptoms, and Russian authorities reported 'no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts'. 'Suspected in media reports' alone leaves out what the authorities have said.

(2) Row 2 should use CDC's exact wording. CDC 'How Plague Spreads' (updated May 15, 2024) says: 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.' It also says: 'Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague' (sick cats are the example). CDC overview (updated Aug 24, 2026) says plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, but these must be given promptly'.

(3) For the calming US fact, CDC's exact line is 'Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.' Don't mix it up with the separate 1924–1925 Los Angeles rat-associated outbreak line on the same page.

WHO's dated risk assessment, as quoted by UN News on Oct 6, 2026, is: 'moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region', and it will be updated as new information comes in. If the script uses it, quote it word for word with the date and speaker. Don't name or picture the worker. Media outlets name her; we don't.
